source.title: A complete solution to the infinite Oberwolfach problem

accepted.question_text: For an infinite group G with no nontrivial involution, characterize exactly which graphs F admit a G-regular solution to the Generalized Oberwolfach problem. Here the Generalized Oberwolfach problem for F asks for a decomposition of a complete graph into spanning subgraphs all isomorphic to F, and G-regular means that the decomposition admits G as an automorphism group acting sharply transitively on the vertex set. The question is broader than the locally finite case solved in the source, because graphs with some infinite vertex degrees may sometimes still be handled by the difference method, while complete graphs cannot be handled that way.

evidence.quote: Given a spanning subgraph F of a complete graph K, the Generalized Oberwolfach problem, or briefly Generalized OP(F), asks for a decomposition of K whose members are spanning subgraphs all isomorphic to F.

A Γ-decomposition of Λ is a set C of copies of Γ such that each edge of Λ belongs to exactly one graph of C. We say that C is G-regular if it admits G as automorphism group that acts sharply transitively over the vertex set.
Open Problem 3.13. Given an infinite, involution free group G, characterize the graphs F that admit a G-regular solution to the Generalized OP(F).

accepted.question_text: For an infinite group G that has nontrivial involutions, characterize exactly which graphs F admit a G-regular solution to the Generalized Oberwolfach problem. Here the Generalized Oberwolfach problem for F asks for a decomposition of a complete graph into spanning subgraphs all isomorphic to F, and G-regular means that the decomposition admits G as an automorphism group acting sharply transitively on the vertex set. The source shows that the involution-free theorems do not extend automatically to this setting, because if G has a nontrivial involution and F is a 2-regular graph consisting of infinitely many odd cycles, then no G-regular solution to the ordinary Oberwolfach problem exists.

evidence.quote: Remark 3.15. Let G be an infinite group with a nontrivial involution i and let F be a 2-regular graph that is the disjoint union of infinitely many odd cycles. Then there does not exist any G-regular solution to the OP(F).
Open Problem 3.16. Given an infinite group G with nontrivial involutions, characterize the graphs F that admit a G-regular solution to the Generalized OP(F).

accepted.question_text: Characterize the infinite graphs F and L for which there exists a solution to the Generalized Oberwolfach problem for F that admits a subsystem relative to L. A solution to the Generalized Oberwolfach problem for F is a decomposition of a complete graph into spanning subgraphs all isomorphic to F; a subsystem relative to L means that, on a subset W of the vertex set, the restriction of the decomposition gives a solution to the corresponding Oberwolfach problem for L. The characterization should cover cases beyond the source's finite-nonzero-degree hypotheses, because the source's theorem assumes locally finite graphs without isolated vertices and then leaves the general infinite-graph case open.

evidence.quote: Here we consider infinite graphs F and L that are locally finite and without isolated vertices. Our goal will be to determine the conditions under which there exists a solution F to the OP(F) over the complete graph KV that contains a solution L to the OP(L) over KW where W is a subset of V .
Finally, we remark that, here, we have assumed the degree of each vertex of F and of L to be finite and nonzero.
Open Problem 4.8. Characterize the infinite graphs F and L such that there exists a solution to the Generalized OP(F) that admits a subsystem relative to L.
